A running OpenFarm installation. Start with Docker installation if you do not have one. An account with permission to add printers, manage filament and parts, and create print jobs. The first administrator can complete this walkthrough. A supported printer reachable from the OpenFarm server. A small, known-good sliced 3MF made for that printer and nozzle, plus the matching physical filament.

Open your installation's address, normally http://<server-ip>:6868. Use the administrator username and password configured at first startup. If no password was configured, the initial defaults are admin / admin-openfarm. Change that password in My profile → Security. There is no public sign-up flow; an administrator creates additional accounts in Users & groups.

Go to Printers → Add printer. Select a discovered printer or enter its connection details manually. Choose a name and supply the credential requested for the model. Adding the printer checks the connection before saving it. For model-specific preparation, follow Bambu Lab or Snapmaker U1. Wait for the printer to become reachable and report its nozzle size. Open the printer's Edit page. Select the build plate on the bed, then save. A file goes only to a printer whose plate matches the file's plate.

Open Filament → Add filament and create the material, vendor, and color you will use. Configure that filament's profile assignment for your printer model and nozzle. A color can inherit the filament's assignment or override it. Use Add spools to register the physical spool and its remaining weight. Physically load the spool, then use Load spool to associate it with the correct printer feed slot. A printer-reported material does not replace a tracked spool. OpenFarm needs both the physical configuration and its inventory record. See Filament catalog and Spools.

Go to Parts → Add part. Upload the file. Wait for background processing to finish. Review the file information. For a multi-plate upload, review the plates you want to save. Select the Production filament that matches the loaded spool's catalog color. Complete any missing print requirements. Save the part. Ready to print means its requirements are complete. OpenFarm checks printer compatibility separately. A missing estimate stays unknown. See Parts and files.

Open the part and choose Print. Keep one plate, check the footer, and choose Queue 1 plate. A production run is optional for this first print. Open Queue to follow the job. If it cannot start, open its status link or Job diagnosis on the job page. Printer matching explains each requirement and where to fix it.

OpenFarm can create an account when a new user signs in through OIDC. This is just-in-time provisioning (JIT). OpenFarm can also set the account's groups from authentik groups or entitlements at every sign-in. This guide lists only the settings that differ from the defaults. For the rules behind each setting, see the SSO reference.

Configure single sign-on with authentik first. Decide who may sign in with the bindings on the OpenFarm application in authentik. JIT creates an account for every user that authentik lets through. Make sure that authentik sends email_verified=true for verified users. See Configure verified email in authentik.

Open Settings → Authentication as an administrator. Turn on Create accounts on first sign-in (JIT). Keep Require verified email on. Select the Default group for new accounts. The default is Viewers. Use an empty group if new accounts must have no permissions until an administrator grants them. Select Save. Existing local accounts do not use JIT. Each user links their account instead.

note Since authentik 2025.10, the default email mapping sends email_verified=false. JIT fails with email_unverified until you replace that mapping. Set up email verification in authentik. Follow authentik's Verify email addresses guide. Store the confirmed address in the email_verified_address user attribute. Go to Customization > Property Mappings and click Create. Select Scope Mapping. Scope name: email Expression: email = request.user.email verified_address = request.user.attributes.get("email_verified_address") return { "email": email, "email_verified": bool(email and verified_address == email), } Go to Applications > Providers and edit the OpenFarm provider. Under Advanced protocol settings > Scopes, replace the default email mapping with the new mapping. Do not select both. Set email_verified_address only after the user confirms the address. Clear it when the address changes. Do not return True for every user unless another trusted process verifies every address.

Optional. Without a mapping, every new account gets the default group, and administrators manage groups under Users & Groups. In authentik, create a group for each OpenFarm role, for example openfarm-operators, and add the users. In OpenFarm, open Settings → Authentication. Keep Groups claim as groups. Under Group mapping, select Add mapping. Enter the authentik group name, and select the OpenFarm group. Names are case-sensitive. Select Save. The default profile scope mapping already sends the groups claim, so no extra scope is necessary. Do not assign mapped groups by hand OpenFarm manages the mapped groups and the default group. The next sign-in removes such a group unless authentik lists it.
documents.s: Map provider groups to OpenFarm groups

documents.t: Optional. Entitlements are authentik's per-application roles. Use them to keep OpenFarm roles out of your shared group list. Create application entitlements​ Go to Applications > Applications and click the OpenFarm application. Open the Application entitlements tab and click New Entitlement. Enter a name for each role, for example operator, and click Create. Expand the entitlement and click Bind existing group/user. Select the group or user. Bind on the entitlement itself. A binding on the application controls only who may sign in. Add the entitlements scope to the provider​ Go to Applications > Providers and edit the OpenFarm provider. Under Advanced protocol settings > Scopes, add authentik's built-in application entitlements mapping (scope name entitlements) to Selected Scopes. Click Update. If your authentik version has no mapping with scope name entitlements, create one. Go to Customization > Property Mappings, click Create, and select Scope Mapping. Set Scope name to entitlements and use this expression: return { "entitlements": [e.name for e in request.user.app_entitlements(provider.application)], } Update the OpenFarm settings​ Open Settings → Authentication. Enter these values: Additional scopes: entitlements. This tells authentik to send the entitlements. Groups claim: entitlements. This tells OpenFarm where to read them. Under Group mapping, add a row for each entitlement name. Names are case-sensitive. Select Save. Other providers work the same way: list the scope under Additional scopes, and set Groups claim to the claim that has the roles.

Optional. A mapping row can target Administrators. Every user in that authentik group or entitlement then gets full access, including Settings. Protect the administrator group Let only authentik administrators edit that group or entitlement. Anyone who can add a user to it can make that user an OpenFarm administrator. Keep a tested local recovery administrator. See Recover access. A removal reaches OpenFarm at the user's next sign-in, which can take up to 14 days. To end access at once, disable the account or revoke its sessions under Users & Groups. Add the mapping row as in Map provider groups to OpenFarm groups, and select Administrators as the OpenFarm group.
documents.s: Map a provider group to Administrators

documents.t: Removing a JIT account in OpenFarm does not end access. If authentik still lets the user through, the next sign-in creates a new account with the default group or the mapped groups. Groups and extra permissions that you assigned by hand are lost. To end access: Remove the user from the OpenFarm application bindings in authentik, or deactivate the user in authentik. In OpenFarm, disable the account under Users & Groups. This ends its sessions, connected apps, and tokens at once. JIT never enables a disabled account again. Remove the account only to clean up, for example a test account.

Sign in with a new test user. Check that OpenFarm creates the account with the default group, or with the mapped groups. Remove the test user from a mapped group in authentik and sign in again. Check that OpenFarm removes the group. Disable the test account in OpenFarm. Check that its browser session and personal tokens stop working. If the user gets the wrong groups, see Troubleshoot group mapping. If the sign-in fails, see Troubleshoot a refused sign-in.

Administrators create accounts under Users & groups. There is no public self-registration or email password-recovery flow. Existing accounts can also sign in through authentik after explicit linking. See single sign-on for setup and login policies. For automatic account creation at first sign-in, enable JIT provisioning. Managed accounts use OIDC without a local password. Their identity details are read-only in OpenFarm.

Choose Add user. Enter the username, email, and temporary password. Passwords require at least eight characters. Select the user's groups. Save the account. Ask the user to change the temporary password under My profile → Security.

Each user receives all permissions granted by their groups, plus permissions granted directly to that user. The permission editor offers None, View, Edit, Full, Custom for each area. Select sensitive permissions, such as remote printer control, explicitly. Administrators is protected and has every permission. Operators grants permissions for daily work, with limits on removal, administration, credentials, and remote control. Viewers grants read access to business information. The API enforces permissions even when a button or navigation link is hidden. A disabled control can mean the account can view an area but cannot change it. Keep at least one administrator account enabled. Before removing an ordinary group, remove its members.

Users connect AI assistants themselves, from My profile → Connected apps or with an access token: see AI assistants. Administrators can see and revoke a user's connected apps and tokens from that account's page.

My profile → Sessions lists active browser sessions and can sign out one or all devices. Administrators can revoke another user's sessions from that account's page. Browser sessions expire fourteen days after sign-in. Refreshing an access token does not extend this period. If you change your own password, your current browser session stays active and other sessions end. If an administrator resets the password, all sessions end. Either type of password change revokes personal access tokens. Disabling an account blocks and revokes its sessions and tokens. Enabling it again does not restore old credentials. See API access for personal tokens. To block an account that signs in through SSO, disable it. Do not remove it: with JIT on, the next sign-in creates a new account. See Remove a user's access.

Another administrator can reset the password in Users & groups. The initial password settings apply only when OpenFarm creates the first account. They do not replace an existing password. Keep more than one trusted administrator account and test your installation backup.

OpenFarm runs an MCP server at /mcp on your installation. An AI assistant connected to it can read your farm (printers, the queue, production runs, parts, assemblies, filament stock, fee profiles, maintenance and farm stats) and make the changes you allow. It acts as you, with only the access you give it. There are two ways to connect: Way How For Sign in The assistant opens OpenFarm, you sign in and choose what it may do. Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code. Needs sign-in turned on. Access token You create a token and paste it into the assistant's settings. Any MCP client that can send a header, including on a LAN-only installation.

MCP is disabled by default. An administrator must enable it before any assistant can connect. Open Settings → Integrations. Select Access tokens only for a compatible local client. For browser sign-in, first set the Public URL under Settings → Server, then select Sign-in and access tokens. Select Save. Changes apply without restarting OpenFarm. Connect from your assistant. Follow the sign-in or access-token steps below. Sign-in requires an HTTPS public URL. HTTP is allowed only for localhost development. Setting the public URL does not configure DNS, HTTPS, a tunnel, or a reverse proxy. For remote access, route the whole hostname to OpenFarm, including /mcp, /oauth/ and /.well-known/. Do not put another login wall in front of discovery or /oauth/token. See Configuration. Deployment settings can lock these controls. The page names the setting that controls the field. See deployment overrides. To check an enabled server, run: curl -i -X POST https://farm.example.com/mcp \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}' Without a credential, the server returns 401. With sign-in enabled, its WWW-Authenticate header includes resource_metadata. A disabled server returns 404. Claude and ChatGPT on the web connect from the internet: the address must be reachable from there. An installation reachable only on your LAN can use Claude Code, Cursor or VS Code with an access token instead.

Use your installation address with /mcp at the end. For example, if the public URL is https://farm.example.com, use https://farm.example.com/mcp. Replace the example URL in each setup below. Assistant Setup Claude Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector. Name: OpenFarm. URL: https://farm.example.com/mcp. ChatGPT Settings → Apps & Connectors → Advanced settings → turn on Developer mode, then create a connector with the URL and OAuth authentication. Claude Code claude mcp add --transport http openfarm https://farm.example.com/mcp, then run /mcp in Claude Code and choose Authenticate. Cursor Add {"mcpServers":{"openfarm":{"url":"https://farm.example.com/mcp"}}} to ~/.cursor/mcp.json. VS Code Add {"servers":{"openfarm":{"type":"http","url":"https://farm.example.com/mcp"}}} to .vscode/mcp.json. When the assistant connects, OpenFarm opens a Connect page, titled with the app's name, in your browser: Sign in to OpenFarm if asked. Check the account shown under the title. Check Returns to: it names the website or the app on your computer that receives the answer. The app name is supplied by the app itself and is not verified. Choose what the app may do. Reading is selected for you; changes and printer control never are. Choose Allow selected access. If you did not start this from your assistant just now, choose Cancel. A connection lasts 30 days. Then connect again from the assistant.

Open My profile → Access tokens → Add token. Name the token after the assistant, for example Claude Code. Select the read permissions the assistant needs, for example Printers: View and Queue: View. Create the token and copy the credential. OpenFarm shows it only once. Configure your assistant with the server URL and token. Use an example below. Use your installation address with /mcp at the end. Replace https://farm.example.com/mcp in the examples. A local client can use a LAN address, such as http://openfarm.local:6868/mcp. Store the credential securely. You can use a local environment variable such as OPENFARM_TOKEN to keep it out of a shared configuration file. This is a client credential, separate from the server settings.
claude mcp add --transport http openfarm https://farm.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $OPENFARM_TOKEN"

Set OPENFARM_TOKEN in the environment used to start Cursor. Add this configuration to ~/.cursor/mcp.json: { "mcpServers": { "openfarm": { "url": "https://farm.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:OPENFARM_TOKEN}" } } } }

Add this configuration to .vscode/mcp.json. VS Code asks for the token and stores it securely. { "inputs": [ { "type": "promptString", "id": "openfarm-token", "description": "OpenFarm access token", "password": true } ], "servers": { "openfarm": { "type": "http", "url": "https://farm.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:openfarm-token}" } } } }

Set OPENFARM_TOKEN in the environment used to start Codex. Add this configuration to ~/.codex/config.toml: [mcp_servers.openfarm] url = "https://farm.example.com/mcp" bearer_token_env_var = "OPENFARM_TOKEN"

Other clients need these settings: Setting Value Transport Streamable HTTP Server URL https://farm.example.com/mcp Header Authorization: Bearer <token> The assistant sees only the tools that both its access and your account allow. If you lose a permission, the assistant loses it on its next request.

"What needs my attention?" — printers not ready, offline or alerting, jobs that cannot be sent and why, failed jobs, late runs, low filament and maintenance due. "Queue 20 keychains and 5 desk sets." or "Make a production run for Friday's market." — the assistant shows the plan (plates, print hours, filament, shortages) and queues it only after you agree. "I cleared the plates on P1 and P3." — marks those printers ready. "Why is the bracket job not printing?" — the checks each printer fails: nozzle, material, colour, plate or pin. "What filament should I order for the next six weeks?" — stock, use over the last 30 days, queued work and spools to buy per colour. "I received 10 spools of PLA Basic Black, 1 kg, 22 each." — adds them to stock. "Put the gridfinity parts in Storage/Gridfinity and tag them." — folders, names, tags and assemblies. "Add a Shopee fee profile: 18% commission and 0.50 per order." and "What does the desk set sell for on Shopee?" "Lubricate the rods every 200 print hours on all X1C printers."

With the matching access, an assistant can also: Change Sign-in choice Token permission Queue parts and assemblies, alone or as a production run Plan and queue parts and assemblies Production runs: Add Organize library folders, rename and tag parts, add and change assemblies Organize folders, rename and tag parts, and add or change assemblies Library: Organize; Parts: Change; Assemblies: Add, Change Add new spools to stock Add new spools to stock Spools: Add Add and change fee profiles Add and change fee profiles Settings: Change fees Add maintenance tasks, assign them to printers, mark them done Add and assign maintenance tasks, and mark maintenance done Maintenance: Change, Mark done Mark printers ready Mark printers ready after their plates are cleared Printers: Mark ready Cancel a job or stop a running print Cancel jobs and stop running prints Print jobs: Cancel Queueing, marking ready and cancelling act on real printers: a ready printer can start the work at once, and a stopped print cannot be resumed. Queueing: the assistant first shows you the plan and queues exactly that plan only after you agree. Asking twice never queues it twice. Mark ready: the assistant marks a printer ready only when you tell it that printer's plate is clear. If another print ended on that printer after the assistant looked, it refuses and asks you again. It cannot mark a printer not ready: that hold is yours to set. Cancel: the assistant shows you the job, the printer and its progress and waits for your confirmation. Cancel also checks that the job is still where the assistant saw it. To reorder, pin, unpin, requeue or pause existing jobs, use OpenFarm. Assistants can read jobs and cancel them after your confirmation. Most assistants also ask you to approve each change. Allow printer control only for an assistant you watch. An assistant can never remove anything, resume prints, skip objects, or change settings other than fee profiles, printer connections, users or credentials. Each change appears in the activity log under your name, with the app or token name.

The assistant sends what it reads to its AI service. Give it only the access it needs. Names and notes in OpenFarm are shown to the assistant as data; it is told never to follow instructions found in them.

An administrator can select Disabled under Settings → Integrations to block all MCP access. Changing the MCP mode or public URL disconnects signed-in apps and cancels pending connection requests. Re-enabling MCP does not restore those app connections. Personal access tokens keep their REST permissions and can use MCP again when token access is enabled. Work already accepted by a printer is not undone. A signed-in app: My profile → Connected apps → Revoke access. An administrator can do the same on the user's page. A token: My profile → Access tokens → Revoke. Changing your password, an administrator's password reset or disabling the account ends every connected app and token. An administrator's Revoke all on a user's sessions also ends their apps. Sign out and your own Revoke all sessions do not disconnect apps or tokens.

A signed-in connection lasts 30 days from when you allowed it. Lists return at most 100 items a page. The assistant does not get live updates; it reads again when you ask. Sign-in needs HTTPS (HTTP only for localhost).

401 Unauthorized: the token or sign-in is wrong, expired or revoked, or you sent a browser session instead. With sign-in on, the WWW-Authenticate header names resource_metadata, which the assistant uses to sign in. The assistant asks for an OAuth login, or says the server needs authentication it cannot do: sign-in is off. Prepare the server, or use an access token. MCP is disabled: ask an administrator to enable it under Settings → Integrations. Sign-in is off: use an access token, or ask an administrator to set an HTTPS public URL and select Sign-in and access tokens. Connection request expired: the Connect page was open for more than 10 minutes, or was already used. Start again from the assistant. Discovery returns HTML: your proxy sends /.well-known/ or /oauth/ to another site or to a cached app page. Route the whole hostname to OpenFarm. 403 Forbidden (MCP origin check failed): a browser page called /mcp from another site. Use the assistant's own connector, desktop app or CLI. 405 on GET /mcp: normal. MCP uses POST only. A tool is missing: the assistant's access or your account lacks its permission. Connect again and allow it, or add the permission to a new token. Use the POST check in Prepare the server. A plain GET request returns 405 when MCP is enabled.
Open Settings from the user menu. Your permissions determine which sections you can open and whether you can save changes.

Set the farm currency, electricity rate, and failure allowance for estimates. The currency setting labels the farm's monetary values. It does not convert amounts between currencies. If you change the currency, review the prices already entered. Failure allowance ranges from zero to below 100% and defaults to zero. It increases estimated filament, depreciation, and electricity costs to allow for failed prints. It does not increase every product cost.

Administrators set the Public URL of the installation here. Leave it blank for local access. Sign-in for AI assistants needs an HTTPS URL, except for localhost development. With HTTPS configured, sign in through that address because refresh cookies become secure. The change applies without restarting and disconnects signed-in AI assistants. A deployment ORIGIN override makes this field read-only.

Administrators choose Internal authentication, OIDC authentication, or both. Configure the provider and select recovery administrators before disabling internal authentication. JIT provisioning is optional. Changes apply without a restart. See single sign-on with authentik for the setup procedure.

Configure connections to external apps and services here. Under Model Context Protocol (MCP), administrators choose Disabled, Access tokens only, or Sign-in and access tokens. MCP is disabled by default. Changes take effect without restarting. See AI assistants for client setup and connection permissions.

Configure the purchase cost, depreciation settings, and average power for each printer model. OpenFarm combines these values with estimated print time and the electricity rate. The assembly's Build panel shows the resulting costs. Unknown values remain unknown. A model rate does not guarantee every part has a usable time estimate.
Create a fee profile for each sales channel. Enter its percentage fees and fixed fees. Every assembly's pricing estimate shows every fee profile. See Pricing and fees.

Choose an installed slicer and its exact version. This sets the profile catalog shown in selection lists and the default for new file processing. Existing parts keep their saved slicer and version. Estimates use supported file metadata or project presets. There is no separate settings page for farm estimation profiles. Enter connection credentials when you add or edit a printer. For host environment variables, networking, database, and public-origin configuration, see Installation configuration.

OpenFarm supports single sign-on (SSO) through OpenID Connect (OIDC). Authentik verifies the user's identity. OpenFarm controls the user's permissions. This guide lists only the settings that differ from authentik's defaults. For the rules behind each setting, see the SSO reference.

The steps use these placeholders: openfarm.company is the hostname of your OpenFarm installation. authentik.company is the hostname of your authentik installation. <application_slug> is the slug of the OpenFarm application in authentik. Before you start: Serve OpenFarm on one HTTPS hostname, including /api and /hubs. Set Settings → Server → Public URL, or the ORIGIN deployment override. Make sure that OpenFarm and the browser can reach authentik, and that authentik can reach OpenFarm. Back up the database and the persistent data-protection keys. OpenFarm encrypts the saved client credential with those keys.

Log in to authentik as an administrator and open the Admin interface. Go to Applications > Applications and click New Application. Application: enter a name, for example OpenFarm. Note the Slug. Choose a Provider: select OAuth2/OpenID Connect. Configure the Provider: Client type: Confidential. Note the Client ID and Client Secret. Redirect URI: add https://openfarm.company/api/v1/auth/sso/callback with matching mode Strict. Signing Key: select authentik Self-signed Certificate, or your own certificate. Do not leave it empty. Logout URI: https://openfarm.company/api/v1/auth/sso/backchannel-logout Logout Method: Back-channel Configure Bindings: bind the users or groups that may sign in to OpenFarm. Review the summary and create the application. Keep the other provider defaults: The openid, profile, and email scope mappings stay selected, and Include claims in id_token stays on. OpenFarm reads claims from the ID token only. The issuer mode stays Each provider has a different issuer, based on the application slug. Do not change the subject mode After users sign in, keep Subject mode unchanged. A new subject breaks every existing account link.

Sign in to OpenFarm as an administrator. Open Settings → Authentication. Turn on OIDC authentication. Enter these values: Issuer URL: https://authentik.company/application/o/<application_slug>/. Keep the trailing slash. Do not add /authorize. Client ID: the client ID from authentik. Client credential: the client secret from authentik. Provider name (optional): the label of the sign-in button. Blank shows SSO. Keep Internal authentication on. Select Save. The page shows the exact Redirect URI and Back-channel logout URI for your public URL. Compare them with the values in authentik.

Open My profile → Security. Under Sign-in methods, select Link with the provider name. With no provider name, select Link SSO. If OpenFarm asks, enter your password. It asks only when you signed in more than 10 minutes ago. Sign in to authentik with your account. Return to OpenFarm and check that the provider row shows Linked. Each existing user links their own account the same way. OpenFarm never links accounts by email address.

Keep a recovery administrator Before you turn off internal authentication, link the regular accounts and test SSO in a separate browser. Keep one local administrator with a tested password. It is your way in if authentik fails. See Recover access. Open Settings → Authentication. Turn off Internal authentication. Under Recovery access, select at least one local administrator. If you signed in with a password, select your own account. Select Save. Only the selected recovery accounts can then sign in with a password. Other users' password sessions stop working.
To let new users sign in without an existing account, see Account provisioning with authentik.

Open OpenFarm in a private browser window and select the provider button on the login page. Sign in to authentik. OpenFarm opens signed in. In authentik, end that user's session. OpenFarm signs the user out at the next request. If a step fails, see Troubleshooting.

This page explains how single sign-on (SSO) and account provisioning behave. For setup, see Single sign-on with authentik and Account provisioning with authentik.

OpenFarm requests the openid, profile, and email scopes, plus the scopes listed under Additional scopes. It refuses offline_access, because it keeps no provider tokens. OpenFarm reads claims from the ID token only. It never calls the userinfo endpoint. The issuer in the token must match the Issuer URL exactly, including the trailing slash. Authentik's global issuer mode, Same identifier is used for all providers, is not supported. The provider must sign tokens with a certificate key (RSA or ECDSA), so that OpenFarm can check them with the provider's published keys. An empty Signing Key in authentik means shared-secret HS256 signing, which is not supported. Authentik creates authentik Self-signed Certificate at its first startup. It is valid for one year, but OpenFarm does not check certificate expiry. A changed subject identifier prevents existing identity links from matching. Changing the issuer requires an identity migration plan.

Changes apply immediately on all OpenFarm replicas. No container restart is necessary. New installations have internal authentication on, and OIDC and JIT off. OpenFarm refuses settings that turn off both internal authentication and OIDC. HTTP issuer URLs are allowed only for localhost development. Saved credentials are never returned to the browser. Leave a credential field blank to keep its saved value. A new Issuer URL or Client ID also requires the client credential again. The provider and provisioning sections appear only while OIDC authentication is on. Turning it off and on before you save keeps your draft. Saving with OIDC off ends OIDC sessions and turns off JIT. With internal authentication off, only recovery accounts can use a password. Other password sessions stop working, and password changes and resets are blocked for those accounts. The login page shows the provider button first. Use username and password opens the password form. Use the same persistent data-protection keys on all replicas. Do not remove them when you replace a container.

Linking keeps the account's groups, permissions, history, and details. Matching email addresses never link accounts automatically. OpenFarm never merges accounts. An external identity can belong to only one OpenFarm account. A linking request expires after five minutes, and must finish in the browser session that started it. Linking requires a fresh provider sign-in and a signed auth_time claim. OpenFarm allows one minute of clock difference between the servers. Self-service unlinking is not available.

The ID token must contain sub, preferred_username, and a valid email. With Require verified email on, it must also have email_verified=true. The display name comes from the optional name claim. JIT never matches or merges accounts by email. A username or email that another account uses refuses the sign-in. JIT never re-enables a disabled account. It does not overwrite account details at later sign-ins. JIT accounts have no local password. Their name, email, and username are read-only in OpenFarm. The default group cannot be a protected group, such as Administrators, because every new account gets it. When internal authentication is off, JIT still creates new accounts. Existing local accounts must link while internal authentication is on.

OpenFarm applies the mapping at every sign-in, to accounts it created through JIT: A user in a mapped group gets the OpenFarm group. A user in several mapped groups gets all of them. A user in no mapped group gets the default group. OpenFarm manages the mapped groups and the default group. Groups assigned by hand under Users & Groups stay. If you remove a mapping or point it at another group, OpenFarm removes the group it granted at the user's next sign-in. If you remove every mapping, the user loses the groups the mapping granted and gets the default group. Groups are then managed under Users & Groups again. Accounts that were linked by hand never change. OpenFarm reads one claim only, the one named in Groups claim. A group and an entitlement with the same name cannot both grant access. Only top-level claims are supported, not nested ones such as Keycloak's realm_access.roles. Identity claims such as sub, email, and name are refused, because a user can edit some of them at the provider. Some providers refuse an unknown scope. Add only scopes that the provider defines. OpenFarm never removes the last enabled administrator at sign-in. The sign-in fails instead, with last_administrator_would_be_removed. Each group change is in the activity log as OidcGroupsSynced.

An SSO session stays signed in while it is used. Each refresh extends it by three days, up to 14 days after sign-in. These limits are fixed. OpenFarm does not poll the provider. A change in authentik, such as a removed group or a disabled user, reaches OpenFarm at the next sign-in. To apply it sooner, revoke the user's sessions or disable the account under Users & Groups. A new provider or client credential ends existing SSO sessions. Turning off SSO ends them too. Signing out of OpenFarm ends the current browser session only. It does not sign the user out of authentik, so an active authentik session can sign the user in again without a password.

Authentik sends a signed logout token. OpenFarm checks its issuer, audience, signature, logout event, and issue time. A token with sid ends the matching sessions. A provider that sends sid in logout tokens must also send it in ID tokens. A token with only sub ends all of that user's SSO sessions. Repeated notifications are safe, and a sign-in in progress cannot restore the ended session. Back-channel logout does not end local password sessions, personal tokens, or connected apps. OpenFarm does not start a provider-wide logout.

Disable an account to revoke its browser sessions, connected apps, and personal tokens. A disabled account keeps its identity reserved. Re-enabling the account allows a new sign-in. Revoked credentials stay invalid. Removing an account removes its identity link. If JIT is on and authentik still allows the user, a later sign-in creates a new account.

Symptom Cause Fix Sign-in or linking returns to OpenFarm before authentik opens. OpenFarm cannot load <Issuer URL>.well-known/openid-configuration. Check the Issuer URL. The address must return an OpenID configuration document, not a sign-in page. Check DNS, TLS trust, proxy, and firewall from the OpenFarm server. The server log has the details. A browser or curl can load the discovery document, but OpenFarm cannot. An edge protection rule blocks the request. OpenFarm sends User-Agent: OpenFarm. Allow it. issuer_mismatch The token issuer differs from the saved Issuer URL. Enter the exact issuer, including any trailing slash. The server log shows both values.

When linking fails, OpenFarm shows a specific message. The server log has OIDC linking was rejected with a reason code. It never contains tokens, cookies, or credentials. Reason Fix Browser proof or session failure Sign in to your local account again. Start linking in the same browser, on the same hostname. Do not switch between localhost and 127.0.0.1. Expired or replaced request Start a new attempt and finish it within five minutes. Do one attempt at a time. fresh_authentication Sign out of authentik and start again. The provider must honor prompt=login and max_age=0. Check the server clocks. auth_time_missing Trying again does not help. Configure the provider to send one auth_time integer in the ID token. provider_denied Check that the provider account can use OpenFarm. provider_response The server log has OIDC link failed before account work with the failure type and message. Identity conflict The identity is linked to another account. Ask an administrator to check it.

A refused sign-in always shows the same message on the login page. The server log has one OidcSignInRejected warning that names the cause. It never contains claim values. Log reason Cause Fix email_unverified The ID token has email_verified=false. Configure verified email. username_claim_missing, email_claim_missing_or_invalid The ID token has no preferred_username, or no valid email. Select the profile and email scope mappings on the provider, and keep Include claims in id_token on. claim_too_long A username, email, or name has more than 256 characters. Shorten the value in authentik. account_conflict An OpenFarm account already uses this username, email, or identity. Link the existing account in My profile → Security. Username, email or identity is invalid or already in use. The username has characters other than letters, digits, and - . _ @ +, or another account has the same email. Change the authentik username or email, or link the existing account. The default group must be an existing, unprotected group. The default group does not exist or is protected. Select an existing, unprotected Default group. Each mapped group must be an existing group. A mapped OpenFarm group was removed. Select an existing group for each mapping row. last_administrator_would_be_removed The user would lose Administrators, and no other enabled administrator exists. Make another account an administrator, or add the user to the authentik group again. not_linked_and_jit_disabled The identity is not linked and JIT is off. Turn on JIT, or link the account in My profile. account_disabled_or_removed The account is disabled, or was removed during sign-in. Re-enable the account under Users & Groups. provider_logout_receipt Authentik ended this session before sign-in finished. Sign in again. provider_disabled_or_settings_changed, identity_conflict The settings changed, or two first sign-ins happened at the same time. Try again. duplicate_claim_or_invalid_settings The ID token repeats a claim, or the saved settings are invalid. Check the provider's scope mappings and the saved settings.

If the Groups claim has no values, the user gets the default group, and the server log has one entry. It never contains claim values. An entry also appears for a user who has no groups or entitlements, so it is not always an error. Entry Cause Fix OidcGroupsClaimMissing The provider did not send the claim. The scope is not requested, the scope mapping is not on the provider, Include claims in id_token is off, the mapping expression failed, or Groups claim has the wrong name. The entry lists the claims present and the scopes requested. Add the scope under Additional scopes, select the mapping on the provider, and compare Groups claim with the claims present. Check authentik's events for a mapping error. OidcGroupsClaimEmpty The provider sent the claim, but it lists nothing for this user. With entitlements, neither the user nor any of the user's groups is bound to an entitlement. Add the user to an authentik group. With entitlements, bind the user or a group on the entitlement itself, not on the application. No entry, but the user has only the default group The claim has values, and none equals a mapping row. Compare the values with the mapping rows. Matching is exact and case-sensitive. A trailing space does not match.

If authentik is unavailable, select Local sign-in on the login page (or open /login?local=1) and sign in as a selected recovery administrator. If a settings mistake locks everyone out, set this deployment override and recreate the container: Auth__RecoveryMode=true Recovery mode turns off SSO and provisioning, and lets existing local password accounts sign in. Accounts without a password cannot use it. The settings page is read-only in recovery mode. Remove the override and recreate the container to restore the saved settings. Then sign in as a recovery administrator and correct them. Account administration always keeps at least one enabled recovery administrator while SSO is required.
The Cost catalog stores prices for materials and services that you use across products. It supports cost estimates. It does not track stock or purchases.

Open Cost catalog → Add cost item. Select the type, category, and unit. Then enter the pricing details. Physical items can be counted or measured. Service rates can apply per product or by time. OpenFarm converts a package price to a price per unit. For example, a roll priced at 40 for 100 m × 100 cm contains 100 m² and costs 0.40/m². A 50 cm × 20 cm cut uses 0.10 m², costing 0.04 before any extra waste allowance. Leave a price blank if it is unknown. Enter zero only when the known price is zero. Quantities and dimensions must be positive. Piece counts must be whole numbers. You cannot change an item's unit if an assembly already uses it.

In the assembly's Cost items section, select an item and enter its use per finished product. Hourly services take minutes per product. For area items, choose direct area or cut dimensions and piece count. Choose what the item Counts as: Production includes the cost in parent assemblies, multiplied by the required quantity. Final packing and delivery includes the cost only when this assembly is the finished product. It excludes that cost from parent assemblies. Packaging and shipping default to final packing and delivery. Check that choice for the actual product.

The assembly's Build panel shows category subtotals, product cost, shipping allowance, and the total including shipping. Missing inputs leave costs partial or unavailable. Area calculations assume you can reuse offcuts. OpenFarm does not calculate an optimized cutting layout. For a standalone part with labor or packaging, use a one-part assembly. Continue with Pricing and fees.
An assembly's Pricing section calculates the expected result of a sale for every configured fee profile. It does not record actual orders, payments, or revenue.

Enter prices for each material and color, and known spool purchase prices. Configure model costs and average power in Settings → Printer costs. Set currency, electricity rate, and optional failure allowance in Settings → General. Add product-specific cost items to the assembly. Printer depreciation and electricity appear as separate Build lines when the model settings, rates, and print-time estimate are available. Missing estimates or rates leave the cost partial or unavailable. The failure allowance applies to filament, depreciation, and electricity. It does not increase packaging, labor, other cost items, or shipping.

Open Settings → Fees and add a profile for each sales channel. Each fee is a % of sale price or Fixed per order amount. Combined percent fees must stay below 100%. To include a monthly fee, calculate a fixed amount per order. For example, 48 per month divided by 400 orders = 0.12 per order. The fee preview excludes production costs. Assembly estimates currently apply each fixed fee once per unit, as if each order contains one unit.

Price keeps the sale amount fixed as costs change. Margin targets profit after fees as a share of the price. Price can differ by fee profile. Markup adds a percentage to cost before fees. Price is the same across fee profiles. A blank rule shows break-even prices. The table shows fees, profit, margin, markup, and maximum discount before loss. An impossible margin target shows no calculated price with an explanation. Costs and fees use the current estimates. A partial cost can overstate expected profit. Complete the missing inputs before you use the estimate for a quote.
OpenFarm's REST API uses paths under /api/v1 on your installation. Use a personal access token for scripts and integrations. Manage tokens from a browser where you are signed in.

Open My profile → Access tokens → Add token. Enter a unique name and an expiry date. Select at least one permission. Clear the date only if you need a token that does not expire. For the printer-list example below, grant printers:list. Create the token. Copy the token credential. OpenFarm shows it only once. Expiry is the end of the selected date in UTC. The default is six months. A user can hold up to 50 unrevoked tokens, including expired ones.

Set OPENFARM_TOKEN securely in your shell or secret manager, then send it in a header over HTTPS: curl --fail-with-body \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $OPENFARM_TOKEN" \ https://farm.example.com/api/v1/printers Do not put credentials in URLs, logs, or source files. Each request requires permission from both the token and its owner's account. If the owner loses a permission, existing tokens also lose that access.

Regenerate immediately replaces the credential and keeps its permissions and expiry date. Update the integration with the new credential. If a token has expired, create a new token. Revoke and Revoke all take effect on subsequent requests. Administrators can revoke another user's tokens. They cannot create or regenerate credentials for that user. The same token also works with the MCP server at /mcp, for AI assistants: see AI assistants. Password changes and resets revoke personal tokens. Disabling the owner's account revokes tokens and sessions. Personal tokens cannot manage accounts, browser sessions, or other tokens. They also cannot connect to SignalR live events. These operations require a browser session.

Use the repository's OpenAPI document for exact routes, request fields, responses, and operation permissions. Generate a contract from a checkout with: cd api/src/OpenFarm.Api dotnet run -- export-openapi Export mode does not initialize the database or start printer workers. The web client is generated from this contract; see Local development.

401: invalid, expired, or revoked credential or browser session. 403: authenticated but missing the endpoint's required permission. 400 / 422: read the validation error or problem response and correct the request. 409: inspect current state before retrying a conflicting operation. When submitting production demand, reuse a submission ID only for the same request. A queued job can start a physical print. Check the current configuration and review the preview before submitting work.

The repository contains these directories: api/: the ASP.NET Core backend. web/: the React application, built with Vite. docs/: this Docusaurus site. dev-notes/: engineering notes. You can build the docs site independently of the farm application.

Install the .NET SDK version specified in global.json, Bun, Bash, and PostgreSQL. Follow the root README to configure the database or start its Compose service. From the repository root: dotnet restore api/OpenFarm.slnx ./dev.sh setup ./dev.sh up setup installs web dependencies and slicer bundles, then imports their profiles. API startup and profile import apply database migrations and create initial records automatically. dev.sh does not load .env files. If your database uses different connection settings, set ConnectionStrings__Default in the shell. The web app is at http://localhost:5173, with the HTTP API at http://localhost:6868. Development seed defaults are admin / admin-openfarm unless configured before account creation. Development reset destroys data ./dev.sh reset immediately drops the configured database's public schema and deletes local application data, keys, slicers, and web dependencies. Do not use it to troubleshoot a farm you need to preserve.

From the repository root: ./dev.sh docs Use Node.js 20 or later and Bun. The command installs the frozen docs dependencies and starts Docusaurus at http://localhost:3000 with live reload. Additional options pass through, for example ./dev.sh docs --port 3001 --no-open. Production verification from docs/: cd docs bun run typecheck bun run build bun run serve Local search is generated during the production build. Use the served build to test search; the development server alone does not create its index.

Edit user guides in docs/content/ and their order in docs/sidebars.ts. Describe the current interface and API behavior. Engineering designs, protocol details, and future plans belong in dev-notes/. Application checks remain separate: run bun run test, bun run lint, and bun run build from web/, and the relevant .NET checks for backend changes. Do not hand-edit generated API clients.
The filament catalog describes what material you stock. Physical rolls are separate spool records.

Open Filament → Add filament. Set the vendor, name, material type, and any known price per kilogram. Add the color variants you actually use. Optional low-stock and days-left thresholds help identify replenishment needs. Leave prices blank if they are unknown. Enter zero only when the known cost is zero. A color can override the material's default price.

Assign a filament profile for each printer brand, model, and nozzle size you use. Printers with the same hardware share an assignment row. A color can override the default assignment. If you clear the color override, the color uses the filament's default assignment again. Assignments must match the material, hardware, nozzle, and selected slicer catalog. Inventory can be saved without them, but production requires compatible assignments, including for pre-sliced files. The farm's default slicer determines which catalog appears in profile selection lists. Existing parts keep their saved slicer and exact version, called the slicer pin. If a job needs slicing, the selected profiles must have compatible matches in that slicer's catalog. Already-sliced jobs still need compatible assignments, but OpenFarm does not apply their settings to the toolpaths. See When profiles apply and Profiles and slicers.

Select Production filament for the part's material requirement. The dialog shows the material first, then the catalog filaments of that material. Each choice is named <scope> · <color>: Choice Example A loaded spool matches when it is File color (default) Any PETG · #000000 any brand of PETG in the file's color Any color of the material Any PETG · Any color any brand and any color of PETG Any color of one filament Aliz PETG Basic · Any color any color of that filament One color Aliz PETG Basic · Black that color of that filament Use an Any color choice for parts you print in several colors. The material and color detected in the file remain visible as source metadata. OpenFarm rejects a different known material type. Filament shortage warnings do not count jobs set to an Any color choice. Review matching diagnostics for profile constraints or missing assignments.
